title: Narrative and dramatic techniques
summary: How prose fiction and drama create meaning through narration, point of view, characterisation, structure, dialogue and staging.

keyterms.definition: The voice that tells a story; not the same as the author.
Narration by an 'I' who is part of the story, giving intimacy but a limited view.
Narration by an all-knowing voice with access to many characters' thoughts.
A narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted because of bias, ignorance or deception.
Third-person narration that slips into a character's thoughts and idiom without quotation marks.
The methods used to create and reveal character: action, speech, description, others' reactions.
Hints of later events that build anticipation or tension.
A scene that moves back in time from the main narrative.
Instructions in a play script about movement, setting, sound and delivery.
A speech in which a character alone on stage voices their thoughts to the audience.
A recurring image, idea or object that develops a theme.
Beginning a narrative in the middle of the action.

questions.prompt: "I'm the most honest person you'll ever meet, so believe me when I say the money just vanished." What kind of narrator is this most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Insisting on honesty while giving a suspicious account invites readers to doubt the narrator.

questions.text: An all-knowing narrator who can enter many characters' minds is third-person ___.
questions.explanation: Omniscience allows wide perspective and dramatic irony between characters.

questions.prompt: "She looked at the invitation. Another dinner with those people. Wonderful." What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Third-person narration slides into the character's sarcastic thoughts ('Wonderful') without quotation marks.

questions.statement: The narrator of a novel should always be treated as identical to its author.
questions.explanation: The narrator is a constructed voice; distinguishing narrator from author is essential to analysis.

questions.prompt: Match the narrative choice to its typical effect.
questions.explanation: Point of view controls what readers know and whom they sympathise with.

questions.prompt: A story opens: "The gun was still warm when the door burst open." What structural technique is used?
questions.explanation: Starting mid-action hooks the reader and withholds context, building suspense.

questions.text: A scene that moves back in time from the main story is a ___.
questions.explanation: Flashbacks reveal backstory and can explain present behaviour.

questions.prompt: Early in a novel, a character casually mentions the river "has taken three children this century." Later a child drowns. The early line is:
questions.explanation: The casual mention plants tension and makes the later tragedy feel inevitable.

questions.statement: Characterisation can be indirect, revealed through what a character does and how others react to them.
questions.explanation: Show-don't-tell characterisation lets readers infer traits from action and reaction.

questions.prompt: Order the events as they are told in this plot: a novel opens at a funeral, flashes back to the friendship's beginning, then returns to the funeral.
items: Flashback to how the friends met
questions.explanation: Non-linear structure lets the ending shape how we read everything before it.

questions.prompt: A character alone on stage reveals her plan to betray her brother. What is this speech?
questions.explanation: A soliloquy gives the audience privileged access to a character's thoughts, often creating dramatic irony.

questions.text: Script instructions such as "(She slams the door. Silence.)" are ___ directions.
questions.explanation: Stage directions control movement, sound and pace; silence can be as meaningful as speech.

questions.prompt: In a play, the stage direction says the lights dim slightly every time the father enters. What is the likely effect?
options: It visually associates the father with gloom or threat
It shows the theatre has a fault
questions.explanation: Lighting is a dramatic technique that shapes mood and audience attitudes to characters.

questions.statement: A motif is a recurring element, like broken glass or birds, that develops a theme across a text.
questions.explanation: Tracking a motif's appearances shows how the text builds meaning.

questions.prompt: Match the dramatic element to its function.
questions.explanation: Drama is written to be performed; analyse it as both text and performance.

questions.prompt: In a novel, clocks appear stopped at moments of trauma. What is this?
options: A motif suggesting time frozen by grief
questions.explanation: The recurring stopped clocks form a motif linking trauma with an inability to move on.

questions.text: The methods used to create and reveal a character are called ___.
questions.explanation: Discuss characterisation through speech, action, description and others' responses.

questions.prompt: Dialogue: "MAYA: Fine. FINE. Do whatever you want." What does the repetition and capitalisation suggest?
questions.explanation: Her words say 'fine' but the delivery shows anger; subtext lies in performance cues.

questions.statement: Stage directions are not worth analysing because the audience never reads them.
questions.explanation: Stage directions shape what the audience sees and hears, and reveal the playwright's intentions for performance.

questions.prompt: Why does an analysis of a play benefit from imagining performance?
options: Because plays are designed to be staged, with gesture, space, sound and silence creating meaning
Because plays have no written text
questions.explanation: Discussing how a scene would work on stage shows awareness of drama as a form.
